overview: Nanzhao was a powerful kingdom centered on the Erhai Lake region of Yunnan, with capitals near present-day Dali. It united neighboring polities in the eighth century and continued into the early tenth. This map record covers only 700 to 800, and its imported outline is seriously misplaced: it lies mainly farther south and omits the Erhai capital region. It should not be read as a reliable boundary of Nanzhao.

periods.title: Unification around Erhai
periods.summary: Piluoge brought neighboring polities together, building on the earlier Mengshe ruling house.

periods.title: Between Tang and Tibet
periods.summary: Wars and changing alliances shaped the kingdom. Its later ninth-century history lies beyond this map interval.

items.text: Nanzhao developed from the Mengshe polity south of Erhai. Piluoge united neighboring rulers with Tang support, but his successors did not remain obedient clients. Geluofeng aligned with Tibet and defeated Tang armies; Yimouxun later broke with Tibet. These changing relationships helped a regional kingdom bargain with two much larger powers.

King Geluofeng erected the Dehua Stele in 766 to explain the break with the Tang court and the relationship with Tibet. It presents the king’s side of the dispute. Later weathering erased much of its lettering, but earlier written copies preserve more of the text. Reading the monument today therefore involves both stone and the history of copying it.

Later, in 829, Nanzhao forces raided Chengdu and carried off prisoners, including artisans and silk weavers. Skills could travel through violent displacement as well as peaceful exchange. The event helps explain why an account of fine cloth or craft techniques must also ask about the people compelled to leave their homes.

The 766 Dehua inscription praises works that controlled flooding and opened land for rice and millet. It also describes draining reservoirs and creating orchards in wet ground. This is royal praise, rather than an excavated engineering plan, but it shows what the court considered a ruler’s achievement: making water support crops instead of ruining them.

The same inscription boasts of households with mulberry plots and government stores sufficient for nine years. Mulberries evoke silk production, while the stores advertise security against shortages. Those sweeping claims cannot be treated as a survey proving every family was prosperous. They tell us what kinds of abundance the king wanted readers to associate with his reign.

“厄塞流潦” means “blocking the floodwaters.” These Chinese characters come from the transmitted text of the 766 Dehua inscription, quoted in a modern scholarly edition. They provide a small sample of the court’s written Chinese, rather than a transcription of an everyday spoken language. Here royal writing celebrates a practical concern that every farming family would understand.

sections.title: Builders, potters and a possible royal shrine

items.text: At Wuzhishan near the early capital Taihe, excavators found courtyard buildings with main halls, side corridors and entrance porches. Nanzhao-period Buddhist images and miniature pagodas helped identify the remains as a temple area. Both the buildings and the objects found inside mattered to understanding its purpose.

Wuzhishan’s eastern kilns contained firing supports, spacers, molds and imperfect glazed pottery. These workshop leftovers show production near the temples. Finished objects tell us what people wanted to make; rejects preserve evidence of work that went wrong. An impressive religious complex also had a practical manufacturing side.

Wuzhishan builders used stone foundations and provided courtyard drainage. One hall occupied two levels, with adjoining corridors and porches. The remains show attention to moving people and water through the site. These are architectural drains; the excavation account does not establish toilets or household sewers.

A tile from Wuzhishan’s Building One carries the characters “官家舍利,” interpreted as referring to royal relics. Excavation director Zhu Zhonghua suggested that the building may have enshrined relics connected with the ruling family. Miniature pagodas and pottery vessels strengthen the religious interpretation, but the royal identification remains a proposal, not a named royal burial discovered intact.

sections.title: Later ninth-century glimpses of family and learning

items.text: The ninth-century writer Fan Chuo describes a major gathering beginning on the first day of the eleventh lunar month. People brewed drink, prepared cattle and sheep, and entertained relatives and neighbors. His account gives shared meals and visits a place in Nanzhao’s social life. The date belongs to a lunar calendar, not automatically to November on ours.

Fan Chuo describes noblewomen wearing silk skirts and jackets, with a square of brocade draped above them. Pearls, gold, shells and amber decorated hair or ears. He also mentions female servants wearing skirts and felt coverings. The contrast is a useful glimpse of household status, though it comes from a Tang outsider’s description of selected people.

He also describes young men making evening music with gourd instruments or even leaves, using the sounds in courtship. A leaf could become a musical instrument without a trip to a shop. This is a reported social custom from the ninth-century text; it does not prove that every community in the kingdom followed the same rules.

Elite young men from Nanzhao studied literacy and numeracy in Chengdu. Historian Shao-yun Yang distinguishes them from Silla students who went to Chang’an and sat Tang examinations. Learning across the border could help Nanzhao’s own government and ambitions. Studying another court’s methods did not require accepting that court’s right to rule at home.

The Illustrated History of Nanzhao, composed in 899, tells a Buddhist foundation story in which Acuoye Guanyin introduces the religion and gives the earliest kings a sacred mandate. It is evidence of how the later court imagined and justified its past. Its divine encounters should be read as religious storytelling, not as independently verified events in the first kings’ lives.

ending.text: Nanzhao’s ruling house was overthrown by Zheng Maisi around 902 to 903, long after the map’s 800 cutoff. Several short-lived regimes followed before Duan Siping founded the Dali kingdom in 937. Political rule changed while settlements, farming and Buddhist traditions continued; Nanzhao’s ending was not the disappearance of the region’s people.
